summary:
Precursor AI is a web platform that turns NASA radar and environmental data into a landslide early-warning map for any area. A user picks an area on the map. The platform finds, downloads and checks the NASA data, measures ground movement with InSAR, and combines it with terrain (NASADEM), rainfall (GPM IMERG), soil moisture (SMAP) and the NASA Global Landslide Catalog. An AI model then forecasts how the ground will move over the next 12 days, with uncertainty shown on an interactive dashboard.

This answers the challenge directly. Landslides often start with slow ground creep and heavy rain, yet most hillsides have no ground sensors. Radar satellite data can see this movement, but it is huge and technical, so decision makers rarely use it. Precursor AI makes it usable: open NASA data in, one clear map out.

In a held-out test at Portuguese Bend, California, our forecast had 10.7% lower error than a zero-motion baseline. This is a research result, not yet a validated warning.

It matters because any region NISAR covers can reuse the same pipeline. We start in the United States, then move to Azerbaijan.
details:
Precursor AI is a web platform that turns NASA radar and environmental data into a landslide early-warning map for any area. The user picks an area on the map. The platform finds, downloads and checks the NASA data, and measures ground movement with InSAR. It then combines that movement with terrain (NASADEM), rainfall (GPM IMERG), soil moisture (SMAP) and past landslides (NASA Global Landslide Catalog). An AI model forecasts the ground movement 12 days ahead, and the dashboard shows it as a map with uncertainty. The pipeline has six steps: acquire, process (InSAR), integrate, analyze, risk and explain, dashboard.

Benefits

Radar data is huge and technical, and most hillsides have no ground sensors. Precursor AI makes the data usable without radar expertise. Every layer is labelled with its source and validation status, so users can see what is real data and what is only a research estimate.

Intended impact

We want decision makers and local authorities to see early signs of landslides, such as slow creep and heavy rain on saturated soil, before a slope fails. The pipeline can be reused in any region NISAR covers. Phase A is the United States, which has lighter data and a well-documented landslide history. Phase B is Azerbaijan, which has terabytes of raw radar data and comes after the pipeline is proven.

Results so far

In a held-out test at Portuguese Bend, California, the forecast had 10.7% lower error than a zero-motion baseline (2.51 vs 2.81 mm over 120,805 pixels). This is a research result, not a validated warning. The dashboard does not issue risk classes, because no validated risk model exists yet.

Tools and technology

- Frontend: Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL for maps, Recharts for charts, and Three.js with GSAP for the 3D Earth.

- Backend: Python, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy and Alembic on PostgreSQL/PostGIS, packaged with Docker.

- Data access: earthaccess and asf_search to reach NASA data. h5py and rasterio read the radar and raster files.

- AI: PyTorch forecasting model (an LSTM-TCN hybrid) run on a GPU. NumPy and SciPy handle the numerical processing.

- Testing: pytest for the backend and Vitest for the frontend.

- Data used: NISAR (planned), NASADEM, GPM IMERG, SMAP and the NASA Global Landslide Catalog. The test forecast used Sentinel-1 OPERA displacement data.

Creativity

The project connects radar processing, environmental data and AI forecasting in one tool a non-expert can use. It is also deliberately honest. It labels every output as research, inferred or not validated, and shows "N/A" where no real model exists, instead of inventing a risk score.

Factors we considered

- Data size: we start with lighter US data and defer Azerbaijan's terabytes until the pipeline works.

- Honesty about accuracy: we tested on held-out data with confidence intervals and report that the model matches a simple baseline in places.

- Safety: the prototype is not for evacuation or operational decisions until it is validated.

- Reuse and trust: every layer records its source and checksums, so results can be traced.

Written for: NASA Space Apps judges, as an added "Scientific basis" section for the project details field. It goes after "Tools and technology".

---

Scientific basis

Our forecasting approach builds on three peer-reviewed studies:

1. Li, Fan, Zhao, Zhang & Duan (2025). Landslide displacement prediction using time series InSAR with combined LSTM and TCN: Xiao Andong landslide, Yunnan. Natural Hazards, 121, 3857–3884. DOI: 10.1007/s11069-024-06937-y. This is the source of our core model. They tested on satellite InSAR data from Yunnan, China. We took the LSTM-TCN architecture: the LSTM captures the long-term trend and the TCN captures short-term changes.

2. Nava et al. (2023). Landslide displacement forecasting using deep learning and monitoring data across selected sites. Landslides, 20, 2111–2129. DOI: 10.1007/s10346-023-02104-9. They used ground monitoring and rainfall data from four landslide sites. We took their way of comparing seven different AI models (MLP, LSTM, GRU and others) under the same conditions, and the Huber loss function.

3. Strnad et al. (2026). A multi-task deep learning approach for landslide displacement prediction with applications in early warning systems. Scientific Reports, 16, 196. DOI: 10.1038/s41598-025-29084-1. They used daily GPS measurements from the Urbas landslide in Slovenia. We took two ideas: a second output that answers "was the danger threshold crossed?", and checking the deep model against a simple linear model.

Our own contribution is applying this approach to open NASA satellite data across a whole area.


NOTE : We deployed it backend on onrender and frontend on vercel and in onrender it has not any free plan to have data in background so the website will not open with the data background. But on local every function works.
